data.title: U.S. drilling rig count slips in latest Baker Hughes survey
data.description:
The number of oil and gas rigs actively drilling in the U.S. fell by 3 to 601 after rising by 1 a week ago, Baker Hughes reported Friday in its latest weekly survey.

The number of active drilling rigs targeting crude oil in the U.S. stayed flat at 463 in the week ended November 13, while gas rigs dropped 4 to 127 and rigs categorized as miscellaneous added 1 to 11.

The total rig count was up by 52, or 9.5%, compared to the same time last year, while the number of rigs drilling for oil rose by 46, or 11%, from a year ago, and gas rigs were up 2, or 1.6%, from a year earlier.

Rigs targeting oil in the Permian Basin gained 2 during the past week to 275, while the Eagle Ford and the Williston Basin remained unchanged at 43 and 30, respectively.

data.title: What a Lutnick Departure Would Mean for Trade, Crypto and Steel — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Joe Light

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appears to be at risk of losing his job after becoming the target of criticism inside and outside the administration for his handling of a company at the center of the Nvidia scandal.

His ouster, if it happens, would have ripple effects on U.S. trade, government-led equity investments and industries far beyond the chip makers at the heart of the controversy.

Lutnick has become a target for failing to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of routing advanced Nvidia chips to China in avoidance of U.S. export controls. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO this week and acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife after reports he had an affair with a onetime Megaspeed executive. The U.S. is investigating that executive over alleged ties to the Chinese intelligence service.

On Friday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC pointed the finger at the Commerce Department for not putting Megaspeed on a list that would have limited its access to U.S. technology. Lutnick plans to testify to the Senate Banking Committee on the issue. Bettors on prediction market Kalshi put 58% odds on Lutnick leaving his post this year.

The White House and Commerce Department did not respond to requests for comment.

Lutnick, the former head of financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald, has been a point person for President Donald Trump in trade negotiations, crypto policy and other issues that intersect with Wall Street. He's also overseen a huge expansion of the U.S. government's direct equity stakes in private companies.

Lutnick's departure would be a blow to a number of industries that he's advocated on behalf of.

In recent months, Lutnick has inserted himself into trade negotiations between the U.S., Canada, and Mexico to prevent tariffs on steel and aluminum imports from being weakened as part of broader trade deals, noted Beacon Policy Advisors analyst Owen Tedford. That's helped companies like Cleveland-Cliffs and Nucor, whose executives have credited the tariffs for bolstering the steel industry.

He's also been a consistent advocate for crypto firms. Lutnick was one of the cabinet secretaries tasked last year with studying ways to increase the government's crypto holdings as part of Trump's "strategic Bitcoin reserve," and had met with executives as Congress considered passing industry-friendly legislation this summer.

Along with Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte, Lutnick has also been an advocate for selling a chunk of mortgage-finance giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

Investors in all three of those industries could be at greater risk without Lutnick at the helm.

Lutnick was also a chief architect of Trump's drive to take equity stakes in private companies. But far from putting a damper on those investments, the Nvidia scandal might put the movement into overdrive.

Since January 2025, the U.S. has announced equity investments worth $30.8 billion across 49 deals, including a near 10% stake in Intel Corp., according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

Many of the investments have been to lessen U.S. dependence on China for supplies of rare earths and critical minerals, notes Raymond James analyst Ed Mills. If Trump takes a more hawkish stance on China after the Nvidia scandal, China could retaliate by limiting rare earths shipments, making those kinds of investments even more crucial.

Increased tension with China "puts more pressure on the U.S. to establish its own supply chain and increases the probability that they double down on investments in those businesses," Mills said.

Write to Joe Light at joe.light@barrons.com

data.title: Bitcoin could fall even further if investors cash out to buy into the Anthropic IPO
data.description:
By Isabel Wang

Bitcoin tumbled below $68,000 on Friday, its lowest level since Aug. 19

Bitcoin could have a new rival for investor cash: Anthropic's IPO.

Wall Street's next big IPO could come at crypto's expense.

Anthropic's (ANT) initial public offering next week may require investors to sell some of their existing assets to make room in their portfolio for what's been hyped as one of the most sought-after stock offerings in history.

Strategists think that could further test the cryptocurrency market, just as Treasury rate BX:TMUBMUSD10Y pressures and other worries send bitcoin toward its lowest level in three months.

The world's largest cryptocurrency (BTCUSD) at one point dropped below $68,000 on Friday, its lowest level since Aug. 19. For the week, bitcoin has plunged nearly 10%, putting it on pace for its worst weekly performance since June, according to CoinDesk data.

Other major cryptocurrencies and bitcoin-related stocks were also getting hammered this week, with ethereum (ETHUSD) down nearly 15% and trading at a three-month low of $1,926.47 on Friday. Shares of Coinbase Global (COIN) were off 5.5% this week, and Strategy (MSTR), the world's largest institutional holder of bitcoin, was 13.6% lower over the same period, according to FactSet data.

"The upcoming Anthropic IPO, potentially the largest in history, could also be drawing capital out of risk assets as investors position ahead of the offering," said Thomas Perfumo, chief economist at Kraken, a U.S.-based crypto exchange.

With Anthropic's IPO coming as soon as next Thursday, investor demand for the shares has already been running six times higher than the number of shares available, according to Bloomberg. To get in on the deal, investors might need to move money out of other liquid investments, such as stocks or cryptocurrencies.

There's a precedent for crypto dropping ahead of mega IPOs due to a temporary liquidity drain, most notably in the runup to SpaceX's IPO (SPCX) earlier this year. Just weeks before that company's $75 billion public-market debut on June 12, bitcoin fell from over $80,000 to under $70,000.

"That could certainly be having an impact here," Jim Ferraioli, head of crypto research at Charles Schwab, said in reference to the selling in bitcoin this summer ahead of the SpaceX IPO.

Bitcoin's slide, just like any asset move, can't be pinned to a single driver. Market analysts said that recent risk-off sentiment across the broader financial market, sparked in part by Nvidia's (NVDA) selloff and the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, also appears to be weighing on crypto.

"The evidence points more to a retreat from risk than a loss of conviction in bitcoin itself, with crypto-specific leverage and ETF outflows amplifying that risk-off move," analysts at Bitfinex Alpha told MarketWatch on Friday. "Bitcoin's weakness has come alongside volatility in technology shares, firmer yields and a stronger dollar DXY."

Higher interest rates can make bitcoin less attractive at the margin. Because bitcoin pays no yield, rising interest rates would make interest-bearing investments, like cash and short-term Treasurys, more attractive by comparison.

However, bitcoin has recently been reacting less to broader economic developments, such as changes in inflation or interest rates, than it has done over the past 10 years on average, said Ferraioli at Charles Schwab. "So these things still have an impact, but less of an impact than they traditionally do," he said.

From a technical perspective, the analysts at Bitfinex Alpha see $67,800 as a key support level for bitcoin, and a close above roughly $68,000 for the week could keep its long-term trend bullish.

"Bitcoin is testing support at its 200-week simple moving average of $67,800, a level many market participants treat as the dividing line between a long-term bull and bear market. Buyers will look to establish a floor here," the analysts told MarketWatch on Friday.

"But a close below the 200-week SMA would suggest that bitcoin is currently trading as a rate-sensitive risk asset rather than a long-horizon store of value," they added.

-Isabel Wang

data.title: NVIDIA Corporation expected to post earnings of $2.47 a share - Earnings Preview
data.description:
• NVIDIA Corporation is expected to show a rise in quarterly revenue when it reports results on November 17 for the period ending October 31 2026

  • The Santa Clara California-based company is expected to report a 91.3% increase in revenue to $109.08 billion from $57.01 billion a year ago, according to the mean estimate from 43 analysts, based on LSEG data.The company's guidance on August 26 2026, for the period ended October 31, was for revenue between $105.84 billion and $110.16 billion.

  • The mean earnings estimate of analysts had risen by about 0.4% in the last three months. ​

  • Wall Street's median 12-month price target for NVIDIA Corporation is $271.00, about 63.1% above its last closing price of $166.19

The company's guidance on August 26 2026 for the period ended October 31 was for gross profit margin between USD73.5% and USD74.5%.
